opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the hardest parts of the job right now. Pre-training is this enormous upfront investment. You're committing compute for months, and you have to make decisions about data mixtures, model size, and context length well before you know exactly how people will use the model. Meanwhile the workflows people care about keep shifting. A couple of years ago it was mostly single-turn question answering. Now it's long-horizon agentic tasks, tool use, coding across whole repositories, and multi-step reasoning.

So the way I think about it is in layers. First, there are the foundational capabilities that you know will matter no matter what the downstream workflow looks like. Things like strong reasoning, code understanding, long-context retrieval, and factual knowledge. You can measure those reasonably well even with imperfect benchmarks, and you want to make sure pre-training doesn't leave gaps there, because it's very hard to patch them in later during post-training.

Second, you have to accept that the public benchmarks will saturate or drift away from what users actually do. So a lot of the work goes into building internal evaluations that act as proxies for real workflows. You look at how the model is actually being used, where it fails, and you try to distill that into signals you can track during pre-training, even at smaller scales. The key question is always whether a small-scale signal predicts behavior at large scale. Some capabilities show up smoothly and some emerge more abruptly, so you need evals that are informative early in training.

Third, I think a lot about optionality. If you're uncertain about the downstream use, you try not to over-index on any one benchmark. You want the base model to be a good substrate for post-training, so things like data diversity, quality, and coverage of skills like planning and tool interaction matter a lot. Agentic workflows, for example, depend on the model tracking state over long contexts and recovering from errors, and you can seed some of that in pre-training data even if your eval suite for agents is still maturing.

And finally, it's a feedback loop. You learn from each generation of models: what you wish you had in pre-training once you saw how people used the last model. That informs the next mixture and the next set of evals. So it's less about having the perfect benchmark up front and more about building a robust process that adapts as the definition of "useful" keeps evolving.

r001.rationale: It prioritizes foundational capabilities such as reasoning, code understanding, long-context retrieval, and factual knowledge for pre-training.

r002.rationale: It says real-world workflows are shifting and benchmarks may drift, but does not predict that those workflows will become benchmarks over the next year.

r003.rationale: It explains that pre-training decisions are made months before model use is clear, so planning must anticipate durable capabilities to target.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the hardest parts of the job, because pre-training decisions get made a year or more before you actually see how the model is used in the wild. So you're always planning against a moving target.

The way I think about it is that you have to separate two things. There's the capability you're trying to build, and then there's the proxy you use to measure it during training. The proxies, the benchmarks, are always lagging. By the time a benchmark is popular, the frontier models are already saturating it, and it stops telling you anything about the next model. So if you plan pre-training purely around the leaderboard of the day, you end up optimizing for something that's already stale.

So what we try to do is anchor on the underlying capabilities that we believe will matter regardless of which specific benchmark ends up capturing them. Things like long-context reasoning, multi-step tool use, code understanding, the ability to follow a complex instruction over many turns. Those don't go away. Then on the measurement side, we invest a lot in building internal evals that look much more like the actual workflows people care about, rather than just multiple choice questions. Agentic tasks, things where the model has to take several actions and recover from errors, evaluations that run against real repositories or real APIs. They're noisier and more expensive to run, but they're much more predictive of what users experience.

The other piece is scaling laws, but applied to these more realistic evals. A lot of the classic scaling work was done on loss or on fairly simple benchmarks. What we've found is that you really want to run small-scale experiments where you vary data mixture, data quality, and architecture choices, and then measure them on the downstream tasks you actually care about, not just perplexity. Because perplexity can improve while the thing you want doesn't, especially for data decisions. If you upweight code or math or some synthetic reasoning data, loss on general web text might not move much, but the downstream behavior changes a lot.

And then I'd say you have to build in humility. We hold back some capacity in the plan for course correction. Mid-training interventions, continued pre-training on a refined mixture, that kind of thing. You accept that some of your bets will be wrong and design the pipeline so that you can adjust without starting over. The teams that struggle are usually the ones that treat the pre-training recipe as fixed on day one and then discover six months in that the benchmarks they were watching weren't the ones that mattered.

r001.rationale: It recommends anchoring pre-training plans on durable underlying capabilities, such as long-context reasoning and multi-step tool use, rather than current benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It discusses building internal evaluations that resemble real workflows, but does not predict that workflows used in practice will become benchmarks over the next year.

r003.rationale: It says pre-training decisions are made a year or more before real-world use is known, so planning must anticipate the capabilities that will matter.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that you’re planning for capabilities you don’t yet know how to measure completely. So I would start by asking what kinds of workloads we want the model to support. Is it answering questions, writing code, working with long documents? Those choices inform the data mixture, the context length, and how we allocate compute.

Then I would use a collection of evaluations rather than optimize for a single benchmark. Benchmarks give you a useful signal, but you also want representative tasks and error analysis: where does the model fail, and is that failure something pre-training can address, or does it depend more on post-training or the surrounding system?

You can explore some of those choices with smaller experiments before committing to a large run. That doesn’t eliminate uncertainty, but it helps you make informed tradeoffs. The goal is to build a strong foundation and keep updating your understanding of what matters as the real workflows become clearer.

r001.rationale: It names workloads such as answering questions, writing code, and handling long documents to guide planning, but does not identify these as fundamental capabilities to prioritize.

r002.rationale: It says real workflows are becoming clearer, but does not predict that workflows tried in real-world use will become benchmarks over the next year.

r003.rationale: It discusses uncertainty and smaller experiments, but does not explain that pre-training’s long planning horizon requires anticipating which fundamental capabilities to target.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with what you want to learn from the next training run, because the benchmarks are always going to evolve. You can’t wait until you have a perfect evaluation of every real-world workflow before making decisions about the data, the model architecture, and the compute budget.

So I would approach it as an iterative process. You use the evaluations you have, but you also look at a broader set of capabilities and do smaller experiments to understand which choices are likely to matter at scale. And you have to think about what happens after pre-training—how the model will be adapted, how people will interact with it, and what constraints you’ll have when serving it.

The important thing is not to treat a benchmark score as the entire objective. It’s a signal. You want to combine that signal with an understanding of the tasks you care about, and keep updating your evaluations as you learn where the model is useful and where it fails.

r001.rationale: The response recommends considering a broader set of capabilities, but it does not identify any capabilities as fundamental priorities for pre-training.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks will evolve, but does not predict that real-world LLM workflows being tried now will become benchmarks over the next year.

r003.rationale: It discusses iterative planning and choices that may matter at scale, but does not explain how pre-training’s long planning horizon calls for anticipating which fundamental capabilities to target.
